Case Studies / No. 03 · In progress

ADHD Buddy Tool

A Canvas plug-in that helps students with ADHD plan their coursework and stay focused through it. A project for my Interaction Design course at UT Austin.

My roleUX researcher & designer
Survey, analysis, storyboarding, wireframes
Team4
TimelineFall 2026
ToolsFigma, Claude, Google Forms
Contents
  1. Challenge
  2. Research

01 · Challenge

Knowing what to do, but not staying on it

Long readings and research papers ask for hours of self-directed focus, on the same laptop that holds every distraction. For students with ADHD, blocking distractions isn't enough on its own. The harder part is managing attention and keeping track of the work.

02 · Research

Asking students how they focus

We surveyed college and graduate students about what they find hard to focus on, what keeps them going and what gets in their way. Responses from students who reported ADHD were analyzed separately from the full sample, since they're who we're designing for.

27survey respondents
14reported having ADHD

We also reviewed research on ADHD and attention, including studies on game-based support and body doubling (working alongside someone else), to check our ideas against what's known to help.

03 · Insights

Structure over stimulation

Four patterns shaped the design, and one of them changed our original idea.

Attention13 of 14 respondents with ADHD struggle to manage their attention, not only with outside distractions.→ Blocking sites isn't enough. Make the work and progress visible.
TasksResearch papers and class readings were the hardest to focus on, each chosen by 19 of 27 respondents.→ Design around a reading assignment as the core scenario.
MotivationVisible checklists (19 of 27) and self-set deadlines (15) were chosen more often than game rewards (11).→ Make a short, editable task plan the core. Keep games optional.
Reminders10 of 14 respondents with ADHD find constant notifications harmful or annoying.→ Work without reminders by default, and let users turn them on.

We started out planning a game-based reward tool. The survey pointed to structure instead, so the game became an optional break rather than the core.

04 · Design

A plan, a focused workspace and a calm nudge

The tool lives inside Canvas as a side panel. It pulls in assignments, breaks them into small steps with checkpoints the student sets, and lets them pick only the screens they need before locking in. If they wander off, a calm block saves the thought for later and sends them back.
